newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says Qatar meeting on, PLO says it's off.
newsitem.headline: Israel says Qatar meeting on, PLO says it's off.

text.p: Israeli officials said on Thursday a Middle East economic conference set for November 16 in Qatar would take place despite a peacemaking crisis but Palestinian officials said it would not.

Israel's Maariv daily newspaper said that at a meeting last week in Washington of Israeli, Qatari, Jordanian, Palestinian, Moroccan, Tunisian, Egyptian, U.S. and European representatives, it was agreed the conference would take place.

An Israeli official speaking on condition he not be named told Reuters: "The meeting took place and there was a decision to hold the conference as planned," adding that it was up to Qatar to issue a formal announcement on the issue.
Officials in Qatar were not available to comment.
Palestinian officials said the gathering -- which would be the fourth Middle East economic conference since landmark peace negotiations began in 1991 -- would not occur.
"This is incorrect," said a senior Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) official, who spoke on condition he not be named.

"No economic conference will be held because we are committed to the Arab League decision to stop normalisation with Israel unless Netanyahu's government declares its commitment to the (peace) agreement and stopping settlements."

Israel-PLO peacemaking was plunged into deep crisis in March when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem and a Moslem militant bomber killed himself and three Israeli women in Tel Aviv.

In April, the League recommended that Arab states stop normalising ties with Israel and restore their economic boycott against the Jewish state. U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross is shuttling between the sides trying to revive peace talks.
Palestinian Deputy Minister for International Cooperation Anis al-Qaq told Reuters: "It is a long way until November. The concentration is more on the starting of the peace process.
"I'm afraid if the situation remains as it is, the peace process in a frozen position, this is going to torpedo attempts for an economic or any other conference."

The last conference in Cairo in November 1996 took place in the shadow of a PLO-Israel crisis over whether Netanyahu -- who took office in July 1996 -- would honour an agreement made by Israel's previous dovish government to hand over most of the West Bank town of Hebron to PLO rule.
Netanyahu -- after months of acrimonious, U.S.-brokered negotiations -- transferred 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian rule in January 1997.
